newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Farmers threaten to boycott Serbia sugar campaign.
newsitem.headline: Farmers threaten to boycott Serbia sugar campaign.

text.p: With only a month to go before the start of the spring campaign in Serbia, sugar beet producers have decided to boycott production deals, an industry official said on Friday.
"Not one single contract has been signed with private farms on sugar beet production," said an official from Jugosecer, the association of sugar producers.
"Without a cash infusion, this year's sugar beet plantings will drop drastically," he told Reuters.
Jugosecer said it expected only 60,000 hectares to be sown to sugar beet this year.
Serbia has planned for a beet area of 100,000 hectares, up from 70,000 in 1996, with cooperatives expected to plant 60,000 ha and private farms about 40,000.
But Jugosecer said only 20 percent of the usual number of production deals with farm cooperatives had been signed so far.
The government late in January outlined a plan to clear its outstanding 800 million dinars debt to farmers, about 425 million of which is for sugar beet.
The government set mid-March as a deadline for clearing the sugar debt.
"Such a programme should have been made in October," said Ljiljana Vasic, head of the association of agricultural cooperatives from the country's bread-basket of Vojvodina.
Farmers said they doubted whether money could be secured by mid-March considering the chronical cash-shortage in the economy.
The association of agricultural cooperatives earlier appealed to its members not to sign any contracts on spring planting with processing firms if they were not paid what was owed to them.
The government expects sugar producers to secure half of the debt by selling products at home and abroad.
"No way will we sell sugar at any price just to get cash," Patkovic Milan, another Jugosecer official, said.
"And we cannot sell it abroad due to lower prices there."

Time for sugar beet producers was quickly running out. "The governemnt must find cash if it wants to maintain production," Patkovic said. "Sugar beet yield drops five percent for each 10 days of delay."
According to the government statistics office, sugar beet production in 1996 rose 41 percent over the previous year to 2.4 million tonnes .
Sugar plants produced 280,000 tonnes of sugar last year, up 120,000 tonnes on 1995, when only 57,000 hectares were under sugar beet.
Vasic said everything now depended on the government.
"Traders, ministries and the entire society must decide if they want to produce food at home or to import."
-- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
